title: Geo routing & control-plane design notes
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures notes and a pragmatic design direction for multi-region traffic steering across Redwood’s control plane and edge: GeoDNS, Anycast, region-preference policies, and failover behavior. The intent is to surface trade-offs, give concrete parameter recommendations, and outline an operational rollout path.

Scope:
- Ingress routing for customer-facing inference endpoints (API and websocket streams).
- Control-plane APIs and distribution for routing policies and real-time regional weights.
- Failure/fallback behavior and observability required for SLOs.

Non-goals:
- Detailed BGP peering configs or vendor-specific router commands.
- Deep dive into egress/data-plane security (TLS/key mgmt handled elsewhere).

Background / constraints:
- Regions: NA-east, NA-west, EU, APAC. Each region runs edge proxies + regional pools for serving.
- Customers can pin to Dedicated or Private regions; hosted customers default to global endpoint.
- We must balance: latency (user proximity), cost (region price differences), capacity (regional saturation), and regulatory constraints (data locality).
- Two main technical primitives available: GeoDNS (region-weighted answers with TTL control) and Anycast (single IP announced from multiple PoPs). Both can be used in combination.

Design goals and acceptance criteria:
- Route most traffic to the closest healthy region with p95 added latency within 20% of local baseline.
- No customer-visible outage on a single-region failure if any region has spare capacity (failover target within 60s-3min).
- Allow operator-defined preferences (cost-sensitive, regulatory, capacity-aware) per-customer or per-route.
- Predictable, observable behavior during rollouts and incidents.

Decision matrix: GeoDNS vs Anycast (short):
- GeoDNS: Pros: fine-grained control per-FQDN, weightable, easier to reason about failover ordering, works with existing CDN/DNS providers. Cons: DNS caching causes slower convergence (TTL tradeoffs), more brittle for clients behind aggressive DNS caches.
- Anycast: Pros: fast failover for BGP withdraws, simple single-IP customer endpoint, client-less reliance on DNS. Cons: less control by region (routing depends on network topology / upstream ISPs), harder to steer by policy, can send traffic to undesired region during route flaps, requires BGP and announced IP space.

Recommendation: hybrid approach by route class:
- Public API endpoints: primary = GeoDNS with low TTL (20–60s) and per-region weighted answers; secondary = Anycast for global fallback (announce reserved IP only from healthy regions).
- Low-latency streaming (websockets): favor Anycast within a region footprint and GeoDNS for cross-region steering because persistent TCP state and NAT behavior favor stable 5-tuple routing.

Control-plane model:
- Central policy service (single source of truth) where operators and automated systems express routing policies in a small declarative language.
- Policy components: region preference list, capacity thresholds, cost weight, regulatory flags, health thresholds, and temporal rules (canary windows).
- Policies are compiled to two artifacts: DNS weight table (per-FQDN per-region weights + TTL) and edge-proxy directives (local weight adjustments, ejection).
- Distribution: use a streaming config bus (gRPC pub/sub) to push updates to edge control-plane agents. DNS provider updates happen via an orchestration plugin that applies weight diffs and validates propagation.
- Versioning: each policy publish creates an immutable version id. Rollbacks use previous version id with an automated canary check.

Policy example (conceptual):
- customer A: prefer NA-east -> NA-west -> EU, reject APAC (data residency). fallback_policy = sequential; capacity_threshold = 70% (don’t send more if >= threshold).

Failover & ejection behavior:
- Active health detection is multi-layer: DNS provider health, edge-proxy health, and regional capacity signals from serving runtime.
- When a region is unhealthy (high error rate or CPU>90%): control plane marks region degraded and applies steering rules:
  1) Reduce DNS weight gradually (from 100% -> 50% -> 10%) over 30–90s to give room to in-flight requests.
  2) Instruct edge proxies to evade local region routing for new sessions (immediate).
  3) If region remains degraded beyond a threshold (configurable e.g., 120s), remove region from DNS answers and trigger Anycast withdrawal from that region for global fallback.
- This staged approach helps avoid flapping and makes failover observable and reversible.

DNS TTLs and weight strategy:
- Default TTL: 30s for hosted API endpoints. Rationale: balance convergence speed and DNS query volume.
- Canary TTL: 20s for canary subdomains during rollouts.
- Weight change cadence: control plane should throttle weight deltas to avoid sudden global shifts (max 30% delta per 30s).

Health checks:
- Multi-probe: TCP connect, application-level (HTTP /healthz returning schema), and synthetic inference sample for end-to-end validation.
- Health aggregation window: sliding 30s with p95 latency and 5xx error rate.
- Use both active probes (from multiple vantage points) and passive metrics from runtime (error counts, queue depth).

Affinity & stickiness:
- For session-based workloads (streaming), edge proxies track session affinity and use source-ip/cookie session keys.
- When steering away from a region, control plane signals proxies to avoid redirecting existing sticky sessions; only new sessions get steered.

Observability & SLOs to track:
- Regional p50/p95 latency, regional request success rate, DNS answer distribution, time to failover (time from health event to >90% traffic shift), control-plane distribution lag (published -> agent ack), DNS provider propagation time.
- Dashboards: per-route traffic map (by region), automated anomaly alerts for unexpected cross-region traffic shifts.

Test plan and canary rollout:
- Unit tests for policy compiler. Integration tests that simulate regional failure and validate traffic shifts in staging with DNS TTL=5s.
- Pre-roll: run synthetic traffic from multiple continents to verify steering preferences.
- Rollout: start with internal-only endpoints (100% internal traffic) -> limited customers -> global.

Operational runbooks (short):
- Regional outage detected: 1) tag region degraded in control plane -> triggers weight-shed. 2) confirm via edge logs and synthetic checks. 3) if persistent, remove from DNS answers and withdraw Anycast announcement. 4) communicate via incident channel and customer notifications if SLA impacted.
- Emergency rollback: publish previous policy version id to control plane which will restore weights and proxies within versioned release windows.

Open questions / risks:
- DNS caching behaviour of large CDNs and mobile carriers can hold answers longer than TTL. How often do we need to fall back to connection-level redirect strategies?
- Anycast blackholing risk during BGP updates and how operators will coordinate with backbone partners.
- Cost model: automated region-preference to cheaper regions may increase tail latency — how to expose this tradeoff clearly to customers?

Next steps / action items:
- Validate DNS provider supports per-record weight diffs via API with <30s apply time. (Owner: Ethan)
- Prototype control-plane policy compiler and streaming distribution in staging; include simulated failures. (Owner: Priya)
- Create synthetic test harness for multi-region failover with configurable TTLs. (Owner: Sofia)

Notes: this is a working doc; expect follow-ups with more formal policy schema and sample config snippets for the SDK.
